title: Block close: the sea
hook: the Talmud is called a sea: no one crosses it, everyone can swim

segments.voice: Yesterday, how to begin, and your line: one line with a partner. Did you ask someone? Today, the long block on the Mishnah and Talmud comes to its shore. Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

Some books get called a library. Some get called a mountain. The Talmud, in Jewish speech, is sometimes called a sea: yam haTalmud, the sea of Talmud. It's a picture of size and of depth, and of something else too. Nobody crosses a sea in an afternoon. Nobody drinks it dry. But you don't have to cross it to be in it. You only have to walk in from the beach. Today closes this block with that picture.
screen: `A LIBRARY? A MOUNTAIN?` → `A SEA.` → `YOU DON'T HAVE TO CROSS IT.`

segments.voice: Look back along the shore we've walked. A written Torah, and an oral teaching beside it, written down when it might have been lost. The tannaim, who gave the Mishnah its words, and the amoraim, who discussed them line by line. The orders: seeds, appointed times, women, damages, holy things, purities. Then how the page works: a case and its voices, a sugya, a question left to stand, Rashi in the inner margin and Tosafot in the outer, the minority view kept for a later day. Then how law is decided: halakha, the way you walk, through the codes to questions about electricity and saving life. And these last days, living with it: a finished tractate, an open page, the ways of peace, hard passages, jokes, flawed heroes, a lost partner, a wounded sage, a teacher who left, and a pomegranate. Now the sea. The picture works three ways. No one crosses it. Even a siyum, the party for a finished tractate, ends with words that promise a return: hadran alakh, we will come back to you. Finishing isn't leaving. Everyone can swim. One mishnah, one line, one partner, and you're in the water; nobody checks your credentials at the beach. And the sea moves. Its currents are arguments that haven't stopped: Hillel and Shammai, a voice from heaven turned away, a question about a bird with one foot on each side of a line. You don't stand outside a sea and admire it. You get wet.
screen: `THE SHORE WE WALKED.` · `NO ONE CROSSES IT.` · `EVERYONE CAN SWIM.` · `THE SEA MOVES.` · then, large: `THE SEA OF TALMUD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to swim a little. Settle, and let the breath move like water, in and out. Bring to mind one thing from this block that stayed with you: a word, a story, a line, a person. Just one. Let it float there. Turn it over once: what does it ask of you today? Don't try to hold the whole sea. One wave is enough. When your mind reaches for more, come back to the one thing, and to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of the block on the Mishnah and Talmud, the sea of Talmud: too wide for anyone to cross, open to anyone who wades in. Today's word.

Your line: the sea of talmud. Today, read one line of Mishnah or Talmud, in any translation, and let that be your swim. Tomorrow a new block begins, with one teacher. Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Jews learn Talmud in many ways: a daily page, a weekly class, a partner, a teacher, a single mishnah. At a siyum, learners often recite hadran, a promise to return to what they finished.
